text: Taeo woke to an empty spot by the bed. Nib was gone. His blanket was folded into a neat square, his mug washed.
He had gone straight to Ryu Survey to show Minho's mother, Seonhee, his new ID. He was a person on paper now. He wanted work inside a gate.
Seonhee gave him tea and warned that he was going blue. 'I'm green,' Nib said.
Taeo burst in with one sleeve on and toothpaste on his face. Where was the note? Nib said he had folded the blanket.
The shouting woke Minho. Who was responsible? Nib pointed at Taeo without hesitation.
Nib wanted the gate with the white stone from Chae's photo. Ryu Survey had won its survey contract: a Grade E gate in the Line 6 tunnel. Entry at ten.
Minho had bid low again. Behind Seonhee, the board was covered in Bluebird notices. One said final.
Minho offered Nib sixty thousand won for the day as spotter: walk ahead, watch for danger, report back.
The subway company hired a clear team, who hired Ryu Survey, who paid Nib. Who did Nib pay? Nobody. Nib went first.
Taeo protested the rate. Nib stopped him. He could count. Sixty thousand was three yard jobs.
And Nib's contract came with insurance. Dokgo's porters earned ninety thousand without it, and paid for their own broken legs.
Taeo got unpaid training at the radio table outside, beside Haein. Nib objected. Work deserved pay. Minho promised wages when Taeo could do the job.
Waiting was the job, Minho's father Dongsik told Taeo, and nobody paid for it. The medic arriving with her coffee disagreed. 'They pay me.'
Im Sejin charged three hundred thousand won to wait at the entrance, six hundred thousand to go in. Either way, she was home by six.
The insurer required a medical. Even for a summon? 'Summoned is not a diagnosis.'
She told Nib to open his mouth. He said, 'You first.' So they both said ah.
She found scars Nib had stitched himself, badly, because nobody else had been there. Next time, she said, there would be her.
Minho's safety film laid out the rules. Crossing into a gate gives you a return mark. It works once, and only to bring you back out.
When the boss dies, the gate's rim flashes and entry closes. Press the mark, and you're out.
Thirty seconds after the boss dies, the mark pulls you back automatically, even unconscious, with everything you're carrying.
But marks don't heal, and they don't revive. Dongsik's hands rested on the rims of his wheelchair.
Nib would get a mark too. But it would bring him back to Seoul, not to the post he was looking for.
Until the boss dies, you walk out on your own. If you can't walk, you wait for a clear team. Dongsik had waited nine hours.
In the van, Taeo asked if matching white stone would lead Nib to his post. It would tell him where to look, Nib said.
At the subway maintenance tunnel, Haein set up the radio table by the violet gate. Sejin took her spot a few metres behind.
The site warden first logged Nib as a construct. His new registration fixed that. This time, the paperwork counted him as a person.
The wooden hauling mule leased for thirty thousand won a month. Nib worked out that his day rate was two months of mule. Taeo wished he hadn't.
Nib refused the boots, and Sejin backed his bare feet.
The radio test dissolved into static at the threshold. The plan: come back out after forty minutes. Nib pointed out that he had no watch.
Taeo stepped up to the frame, scared, and knocked twice. Nib would be ahead of everyone. Taeo wanted something to come back, even a sound.
Sound could pass through at close range, Sejin said. So Taeo made a code. Two knocks from outside: come back. Three from inside: coming.
Then he started adding more warnings. Nib cut in and repeated the code perfectly. He had understood the first time.
Before going, Nib pressed his palm to the steel frame. Taeo felt the amber pulse answer in his own hand.
Nib stepped through, a white return mark closing around his wrist. Grandpa had warned Taeo never to go in. He had never said what to do when someone else did.
The mule followed, then Minho. Taeo held out his trembling hand. The amber pulse went dark.
